name: Lip balm / petrolatum slugging

lead: Lip balm and petrolatum keep lips soft, less cracked and less flaky, so they look smoother and healthier. It is routine lip care and the usual first-line approach for chapped lips.

Waxes and petrolatum are occlusives that slow water loss from the lip surface, while oils and butters soften it. Dermatology references describe simple chapped lips as usually responding to barrier lubricants such as balm or petroleum jelly. Applying a thick layer overnight is called slugging in skincare culture. Appearance trials are not a focus of research.

paras: People apply balm through the day and a thick layer of petrolatum at night. It pairs with avoiding lip licking and with sun-protective balms outdoors. Chapped lips often improve within a few days of consistent use.

Contact allergy to ingredients such as beeswax, propolis, carnauba wax and peppermint oil is documented. Petroleum jelly can contain mineral oil hydrocarbons, which a German consumer group flagged in 2015.

angle.text: Users apply balm or a thick layer of petrolatum to seal in moisture, keeping lips soft, less cracked and less flaky. It is routine lip care with a documented barrier effect, and appearance trials on it are not a focus of research.

lead: Lip balm is a wax-based topical product that forms an occlusive layer over the lips to seal in moisture and relieve chapping. Common bases include beeswax, carnauba or candelilla wax, lanolin, paraffin and petrolatum, sometimes with flavor, color, camphor or sunscreen.[1][2] Petrolatum (petroleum jelly) used alone is a widely used skin protectant, and applying a thick layer as the last step of an evening routine is called slugging in skincare culture.[3][4][4]

People use lip balm and petrolatum to keep lips smooth, soft and free of flaking, which makes the lips look fuller and healthier, and slugging is used the same way on the face to give a hydrated, glossy finish by morning. Dermatology references describe simple chapped lips as usually responding to barrier lubricants such as lip balm or petroleum jelly.[5] A review of lip-licking dermatitis recommends a bland lip balm with ultraviolet protection among practical daily interventions.[6]

Slugging spread through TikTok and skincare media in the early 2020s, and a 2022 Clinics in Dermatology analysis of the 50 most-viewed slugging videos found dermatology professionals produced more of the educational content than influencers did.[4] A 2024 Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology review of petroleum jelly covers its history, uses, flammability, allergenicity and comedogenicity.[4] A 2025 within-person randomised trial compared petrolatum with extra virgin olive oil on the forearm and found petrolatum had the stronger occlusive effect.[4]

In looksmaxxing communities, lip balm appears as a basic grooming item, one thread claims it can be used on eyebrows to make them look thicker, and another recommends petrolatum on the face as a shine step.[7][8] Case reports document allergic contact reactions to lip balm ingredients including beeswax, propolis, carnauba wax and peppermint oil,[9][10][11] and some physicians and dermatologists have debated whether certain balms worsen dryness.[2]

Petroleum jelly refined and patented by Robert Chesebrough, 1872[3]

paras: Lip balms are sold as sticks, pots or liquids. Their structure comes from waxes, with oils and butters such as shea, cocoa, coconut and jojoba added for emolliency, and occlusives such as petrolatum to reduce water loss; antioxidants like vitamin E are often added.[1][2] Medicated types may include camphor or menthol, and sunscreen balms contain UV filters.[1]

Petroleum jelly is a semi-solid mixture of hydrocarbons, mainly with carbon numbers above 25. It is colourless to pale yellow, insoluble in water and melts between about 40 and 70 degrees Celsius depending on the blend.[3] Brands that sell lip balm or petrolatum-based products include Burt's Bees, Blistex, Carmex, ChapStick, Labello, Lip Smacker, EOS, Vaseline, Aquaphor and Nivea.[2]

The Egyptians are reported to have used beeswax, olive oil and animal fat to protect the lips as early as 40 BC.[2] Physician Charles Browne Fleet developed ChapStick in the 1880s and sold the rights in 1912 to John Morton for $5.[2] Alfred Woelbing created Carmex in Milwaukee in 1937 for cold sores, Bonne Bell released the first flavoured balm under the Lip Smacker name in 1973, and Burt's Bees launched its beeswax balm in 1991.[2]

Petroleum jelly traces back to 1859, when workers on early US oil rigs noticed a paraffin-like residue that they used on cuts and burns. Chemist Robert Chesebrough refined it, patented the process in 1872 (US patent 127,568) and sold it as Vaseline.[3] The global lip balm market was valued at about US$732.76 million in 2022 and was projected to reach about $1.25 billion by 2027; in 2019 US unit sales, ChapStick led, followed by Carmex and Burt's Bees.[2]

Petrolatum is described as a skin protectant that reduces transepidermal water loss, the passive evaporation of water through the outer skin layer, which is why it is used to prevent chapped hands and lips and to soften cuticles.[3] Occlusive products sit on the surface rather than adding water, so dermatology texts describe them as most effective when applied over already-hydrated skin.[3][4]

In the 2025 randomised within-person trial of 54 healthy adults, extra virgin olive oil and petrolatum were applied to separate areas of the forearm. Both improved hydration and reduced redness and skin temperature, but only petrolatum also lowered water loss, and petrolatum had the stronger effect on skin surface microtopography markers such as desquamation, while olive oil promoted early-stage cell renewal.[4]

The 2024 JAAD review describes petrolatum as a staple vehicle for medicated ointments, a patch-test instrument and a wound-care product, and states that it addresses two common myths: that petrolatum is unsafe around oxygen and that it causes acne.[4] The Wikipedia article adds that the American Academy of Dermatology recommends keeping skin injuries moist with petroleum jelly to reduce scarring.[3]

Slugging means applying a thick layer of a petrolatum-based ointment to the face as the final step of an evening routine so that moisture stays in overnight, and the 2022 Clinics in Dermatology paper describes it as a TikTok beauty trend.[4] Wikipedia cites a 2022 USA Today piece on the viral trend.[3]

Pagani and colleagues screened the 50 top TikTok videos on slugging. About 37 percent were educational; health care providers made proportionally more educational videos (87.5 percent), while influencers made more patient-experience videos (43.3 percent), and providers' videos scored higher on the DISCERN information-quality measure (median 3 versus 2).[4] The authors note that because the ointment is occlusive, the practice has a potential risk for harm.[4]

Proponents describe slugging as a way to leave dry or flaky skin looking smoother and glossier by morning. In the male-grooming corner of looksmaxxing, a looksmax.org poster suggests applying Vaseline to a still-damp face for shine and calls it 'makeup for men', while a reply predicts breakouts.[8] The JAAD review's position is that petrolatum itself is not comedogenic, whereas the 2022 paper's authors flag occlusion as the potential source of problems.[4][4]

Petroleum jelly forms a barrier that slows moisture loss and can prevent chapped lips.[3] Slugging refers to applying a thick layer to the face before bed to lock in moisture overnight; Wikipedia cites a 2022 USA Today piece on the viral trend.[3] Wikipedia also notes that the American Academy of Dermatology recommends keeping skin injuries moist with petroleum jelly to reduce scarring.[3]

Wikipedia notes that petroleum jelly can contain mineral oil aromatic hydrocarbons; in 2015 the German consumer organization Stiftung Warentest reported levels up to 9% in some Vaseline products and advised against mineral-oil products for lip care, while a 2017 study reported up to 1% and the EU caps polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in cosmetics at 0.005%.[2][3] A 2012 European Food Safety Authority opinion described mineral oil aromatic hydrocarbons as potentially carcinogenic.[3]

Beyond the basic stick, balms are sold with sunscreen filters, tints, flavours and medicated ingredients such as camphor or menthol.[1][2] Petrolatum-based ointments such as Vaseline and Aquaphor are used both as lip balm and as the slugging layer.[2] Sunscreen balms are relevant because lip-licking dermatitis reviews list UV-protective balms among daily measures.[6]

The Wikipedia article describes EOS introducing a spherical balm in 2011 and the 2013 'beezin' practice of applying Burt's Bees to the eyelids, which went viral on TikTok in 2022 and which Wikipedia notes can irritate the eyes.[2] Specific medical lip products include DNA repair enzyme balms for actinic cheilitis and dexpanthenol treatments for isotretinoin cheilitis.[12][13][14]

A 2020 report in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science examined the efficacy of a highly occlusive formulation for dry lips.[15] A 2015 study abstract in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology followed 32 women over two weeks of balm use and reported improved lip condition and hydration lasting about eight hours; Wikipedia notes it was entirely funded by Burt's Bees.[2]

For specific lip problems, trials have examined medicated approaches: a pilot study of 29 patients with actinic cheilitis used a DNA repair enzyme lip balm twice daily for three months,[12] and studies have examined dexpanthenol lip mesotherapy for isotretinoin-induced cheilitis.[13][14]

Contact allergy to beeswax and propolis has been studied among patients with cheilitis or facial dermatitis.[9] Case reports describe acute allergic contact dermatitis of the lips from peppermint oil in a lip balm[10] and allergy to propolis and carnauba wax from lip balm in a child.[11] A review of allergic contact dermatitis from men's personal care products lists lip balm among the products implicated.[16]

Some physicians have suggested certain balms are addictive or contain drying ingredients, but professionals dispute this, and manufacturers deny it; alternative explanations offered include lip licking, weather, mouth breathing and a learned preference for the feel.[2] Lip licking is also described as a common cause of cheilitis, and a review of lip-licking dermatitis lists cheilitis simplex, angular cheilitis and exfoliative cheilitis among its sequelae.[5][6] Peppermint oil used in some balms is an eye irritant that can cause dermatitis if applied to eyelids.[2]

ChapStick tubes concealing hidden microphones were used in the Watergate scandal, according to Wikipedia, and cannabis-infused balms have appeared where cannabis is legal.[2] The practice called beezin, dating to 2013, involves applying Burt's Bees balm to the eyelids and went viral on TikTok in 2022.[2]

On looksmax.org, users discuss petrolatum as a facial finishing step: one thread suggests rubbing the face with ice to reduce bloating and applying Vaseline while the skin is still wet for a shine, calling it makeup for men, while a reply says it would make them break out.[8]

No studies found testing lip balm or slugging for cosmetic appearance in the looksmaxxing sense. Related published work includes a within-person randomised trial of 54 adults comparing petrolatum and olive oil on forearm barrier function,[4] a 2020 report on a highly occlusive formulation for dry lips,[15] a pilot study of 29 patients with actinic cheilitis using a DNA repair enzyme lip balm for three months,[12] contact-allergy studies and case reports,[9][10][11] and a study of the quality and safety of commonly used cosmetic preparations drawing on 447 survey responses.[17]

A 2015 abstract in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology followed 32 women aged 20 to 40 over two weeks of balm use and reported hydration lasting about eight hours and improved barrier function; Wikipedia notes that it was funded by Burt's Bees.[2] A content analysis of social media posts about slugging is a study of videos rather than of skin outcomes.[4]

lore.intro: Lip balm is discussed as a basic upkeep item, with occasional off-label ideas such as eyebrow use and petrolatum as a facial shine; slugging itself is discussed mostly on TikTok and in skincare media rather than on looksmaxxing forums.[7][8][4]

claims.claim: Lip balm can make eyebrows look thicker.
Vaseline on a damp, iced face gives a glossy finish like makeup.
Petrolatum slugging locks in moisture overnight.
Petroleum jelly is a carcinogenic contaminant risk.
Slugging gives skin a smoother, glowier look by morning.
Viral slugging videos are reliable guidance.
